meaning: A way to log in with your password plus a second proof, like a code texted to you. A stolen password alone won't work.
clues: To get in, you must show two different kinds of proof, such as something you know and something you have.
One common second proof is a code sent to your phone.
Even if a crook steals your password, they still can't get in without the second proof.
It's not usually turned on for you. You switch it on in your account settings.
Its name starts with the letter T and ends with a word that means signing in.
assumes: A security question is one extra question that you answer from memory
A screen lock is a PIN, passcode or fingerprint that opens your phone
Single sign-on is one login used for many apps

decoys.meaning: A personal question you answer to prove who you are or to reset a password.
Locks your phone's screen when you're not using it. You open it with a PIN, passcode or fingerprint.
One account that lets you get into many apps without signing in again for each one.

exchange.speaker: bud
exchange.text: Try it with someone you trust. Open your email's settings and look for two-factor or two-step. The FTC says to start with your most sensitive accounts, like email and your bank.

exchange.speaker: floyd
exchange.text: Our bank cards worked this way. You needed the card and a PIN only you knew. Two things beat one.

exchange.speaker: bud
exchange.text: Right. And if someone contacts you first and asks for the code, don't share it.

sources.name: CISA, Protect Our World with MFA
FTC, how to protect your phone from hackers

blank.sentence: Even with her stolen password, the crook could not get in, because her ___ also needed a code texted to her phone.

why: It keeps your account safe even if someone steals your password.

situations.text: A caller says they work for your email company and asks you to read out the code that was just texted to you.
situations.why: Never share a code with someone who contacts you first.
